item.content:encoded:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

item.content:encoded:
As far as Howie Rose is concerned, this isn’t goodbye. At least not yet.
The longtime radio voice of the New York Mets called his final game for the Metropolitans on Sunday — a 7-2 Phillies win — and as he called a ninth inning for the final time, the timeless sound of the Beatles echoed throughout Citi Field. Rose, a self-diagnosed Beatlemaniac who even left the booth mid-game this season to share pleasantries with Sir Paul McCartney, didn’t let the song’s title — “Hello, Goodbye” — be the last words he ushered into this new era of Mets baseball.
“It’s not goodbye as far as I’m concerned,” Rose said on air, as fans in the stadium chanted his name loud enough to hear over the broadcast. “I’ll still be here for the ceremonies, and I don’t mean the retirement ceremonies. I mean Opening Day, and when we have Mets Hall of Fame Day, or retire a number, have an Old Timers’ Day. So I’m stepping away. It’s basically a retirement.”
An emotional Howie Rose reacts to Mets fans chanting his name as he begins his final inning: pic.twitter.com/YuB9Pvmvro
— WFAN Sports Radio (@WFAN660) September 20, 2026
Rose has previously left the door open to calling an occasional game after stepping away for good, saying last month he could see himself dropping in for one or two once he’s officially retired. But Sunday still carried some sort of finality, the culmination of a farewell Rose had already begun articulating a day earlier, hedging against a forecast that threatened to wash out Sunday’s finale.
“Whether they play tomorrow or not, I just preemptively want to say how much you all mean to me,” he told listeners Saturday, calling Mets fans “kindred spirits” who could just as easily be sitting in his chair, having grown up, like him, in the upper deck of Shea Stadium.
While the Mets pushed Rose’s formal ceremony to next season, Sunday’s game went on as scheduled anyway, giving Rose his actual final broadcast.
In honor of Howie Rose calling his last game, the Mets collectively tipped their hats towards the radio booth 🥹
“Fitting tribute for a legend” – Gary Cohen pic.twitter.com/HXwscTl04e
— SNY (@SNYtv) September 20, 2026
The Mets entered 2026 with the since fired Carlos Mendoza texting Rose in spring training to promise this would finally be his year, the World Series parade that had eluded both the team and its 52-year broadcaster. Instead, the Mets spent the year settling for far less than that vision, and Rose, whose ongoing battle with bladder cancer kept him off the road this season, called every one of his final home games anyway, unwilling to miss a single one. It was a quieter final chapter than the one he authored just two years earlier, when his calls of Francisco Lindor’s and Pete Alonso’s postseason home runs during the Mets’ 2024 NLCS run became the signature calls of his career.
While Rose certainly deserved better than a rain-postponed ceremony and a season that fell short of the World Series ending he’d hoped for, he closed out Sunday’s broadcast the way he’s closed out thousands of others: thanking his broadcast partners, his producers, and the fans who’d spent decades in the car, at the beach, or hiding a radio under the covers during a late West Coast game.
@Mets Hall of Fame Radio Voice Howie Rose says his Final Goodbye! pic.twitter.com/T4ZNZCA15j
— Mets Radio 880 (@metsradio880) September 20, 2026
“So for Keith, Ed and Pat McCarthy, I’m Howie Rose,” he said. “Thanks for joining us once again.”

item.content:encoded:
You know that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ offseason has officially arrived when we’re talking about a potential Paul Skenes trade.
It’s been a bit, hasn’t it? The Pirates remained in NL Wild Card contention throughout the second half, which ordinarily would be enough to halt the annual speculation. But Skenes has looked nothing like his Cy Young self, and he could realistically end the year with an ERA above 4.00. This is the same pitcher who had a 1.96 ERA through his first 320.2 innings and looked unhittable most nights.
In the grand scheme of things, nothing has changed. Skenes hasn’t publicly requested a trade, and the Pirates have insisted they won’t trade the three-time All-Star. Objectively, we imagine he’ll be toeing the mound on Opening Day 2027, whenever that might be.
Bleacher Report’s Zachary D. Rymer nonetheless pitched (pun intended) two possible Skenes trades, one involving the Yankees and another featuring Mets. Needless to say, we have plenty of thoughts.
Yankees send Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and two pitchers to the Pirates for Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: C+
Yankees grade: C-
Those who spend much of their free time scrolling X/Twitter (hey, we know the feeling all too well) are likely familiar with the meme of Bugs Bunny squinting his eyes and saying “No.” That’s exactly how we felt upon initially seeing this trade offer.
Let’s start with the obvious: the Yankees aren’t trading Rice. At no point did we hear his name floated amid the Tarik Skubal rumors, and his left-handed power makes him a perfect fit for Yankee Stadium’s short porch. He’ll either open next season as the starting first baseman or designated hitter, depending on what Giancarlo Stanton’s future looks like; the 2017 NL MVP has one year left on his deal, and he’s been an injury liability since the start of 2019.
We’re skeptical that Jones would be moved unless the return involves an MVP-caliber outfielder. Trent Grisham is a pending free agent, and we’re genuinely unsure what Jasson Domínguez’s future in New York looks like, especially after his recent demotion to Triple-A. When a team doesn’t want you on the big-league roster ahead of the playoffs, what does that say?
Reynolds has had a fine year, and he entered Sunday leading the league in doubles. But if you’re the Yankees, do you really want to give up Jones and Lagrange for an outfielder who turns 32 in January? Reynolds is under contract through 2030 (with a $20 million team option for 2031), and that’s a significant commitment to someone who, at his best, is a mid-3 bWAR player.
We must also note that Rymer claimed that Rodríguez ranked No. 82 and Lagrange placed No. 100 on MLB Pipeline, which is simply untrue. Shortstop Dax Kilby is the only Yankees player on the most recent MLB Pipeline list, and he placed No. 83. So the Pirates wouldn’t even be landing a top-100 prospect? Hard pass.
That said, we’ll give the Yankees a C- for their return, because an elite Skenes ranks among the game’s best pitchers. But will we see him regain that 2024-25 form? That we’re even asking the question should say enough.
Mets give up Carson Benge and two prospects for Pirates teammates Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: D
Mets grade: C
At least the proposed Pirates-Yankees trade made some sense. We can’t say the same about Pittsburgh theoretically shipping Skenes and Reynolds to the Mets for Benge, Rojas, and Tong.
First off, why would the Mets only need to give up three players rather than the Yankees’ four? Rymer listed Rojas as the No. 79 prospect and Tong at No. 88, neither of which is accurate; Rojas is No. 73, and MLB Pipeline no longer lists Tong among its top 100 prospects, for reasons we don’t understand. Mariners lefty Kade Anderson has thrown 25.1 big-league innings, and he's still ranked No. 5, but Tong and his 39.2 innings over two seasons no longer qualify. Huh?
Benge has quietly enjoyed a solid rookie season, hitting .276 with 19 home runs, 61 RBIs, 22 steals, and a .760 OPS through his first 149 games. But for him to be the centerpiece of a deal involving both Skenes and Reynolds is absurd. Oh, and Benge turns 24 in January, so he’d be a slightly older second-year starter.
As for the Mets, adding yet another long-term contract isn’t the answer to putting their disastrous 2026 season behind them. As we’ve said before, Bo Bichette would be foolish to exercise his opt-out clause and leave $42 million in guaranteed money on the table. Marcus Semien has two years and $46 million left on his deal, and we’re not even factoring in Francisco Lindor’s contract.
That said, we’ve seen enough positives from Benge thus far to hold off on giving the Pirates’ theoretical return an “F” grade. But both teams should pass on even contemplating such an offer.

item.content:encoded:
Francisco Lindor and Manny Machado continue to be two of the highest-paid infielders in Major League Baseball, both signed to nine-figure, long-term contracts. Lindor’s deal with the New York Mets extends through 2031, while Machado’s extension with the San Diego Padres extends through 2033.
The financial comparison is more than headline contract values. Their net worth includes their 2026 salary and all career earnings in MLB, as well as endorsements, investments and real estate holdings. However, specific personal net worth figures are not publicly available and are subject to estimation, not official disclosure.
Francisco Lindor and Manny Machado net worth comparison in 2026
Francisco Lindor and Manny Machado are also in the same ballpark of wealth, according to public estimates, in 2026. Lindor’s deal with the Mets has greatly boosted his wealth, while Machado has built up big earnings thanks to his contracts with the Padres and his previous MLB deals.
Celebrity Net Worth reports that Lindor’s current deal is for $341 million over 10 years, and it keeps him signed through the 2031 season. The deal Machado signed is bigger in total value at $350 million over 11 years and runs through 2033, according to Celebrity Net Worth.
| Financial category | Francisco Lindor | Manny Machado |
| Estimated net worth | $75M–$100M | $75M–$100M |
| Current MLB team | New York Mets | San Diego Padres |
| Current contract | 10 years, $341M | 11 years, $350M |
| Contract through | 2031 | 2033 |
| 2026 total salary/payroll figure | $32.48M | $25.09M |
| Average annual value | $34.1M | $31.82M |
Lindor’s financial foundation is a 10-year, $341 million deal with the Mets. Celebrity Net Worth said the deal averages $34.1 million a year and was designed to keep the All-Star shortstop in New York through the 2031 season.
According to Celebrity Net Worth, Lindor is ranked as one of the highest-paid players in Major League Baseball in 2026 with a total compensation of approximately $32.48 million. Career earnings projections have also climbed above $200 million, a nod to his time with Cleveland and New York.
Manny Machado wealth profile with San Diego Padres
Machado’s wealth comes from an elite MLB career and successive blockbuster contracts. Per Celebrity Net Worth, the Padres finalised his 11-year, $350 million extension in February 2023, keeping him in San Diego through the 2033 season.
The average annual value of the contract is approximately $31.82 million. His reported 2026 salary is about $25.09 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth. But the contract structure boosts his salary in later seasons, with Baseball-Reference listing an average of $39.1 million per year from 2027 to 2033.
Machado’s financial portfolio is not just his playing salary. His long career in the MLB, along with endorsements and property holdings, has helped establish other sources of wealth, although specific private investments and asset values are not fully disclosed.
Lindor and Machado contract earnings compared in 2026
The headline numbers give you a sense of how close the two financial profiles are, but they also reveal an important difference in the structure of the contract. Machado has the larger overall commitment at $350 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth, but Lindor has the larger average annual value at $34.1 million.
Lindor is also making more in 2026 than Machado is reportedly making. Celebrity Net Worth has Lindor’s AP-derived salary data at about $32.48 million for the season and Machado’s at $25.09 million.
| Contract and earnings category | Francisco Lindor | Manny Machado |
| Total current contract | $341M | $350M |
| Contract length | 10 years | 11 years |
| Average annual value | $34.1M | $31.82M |
| 2026 compensation | $32.48M | $25.09M |
| Contract expiration | 2031 | 2033 |
| Major MLB position | Shortstop | Third baseman |
That means the two are still among the highest-paid players in baseball. Lindor’s deal has the higher average salary, while Machado’s contract has the higher guaranteed amount and that extra year of contractual security. Their future net worths will also depend on taxes, spending, investment performance, endorsements and the value of assets accumulated from their careers.

item.content:encoded:
Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor understands how momentous Saturday at Citi Field is.
The organization is honoring Carlos Beltrán by inducting him into the Mets Hall of Fame and retiring his No. 15. Beltrán is a player who not only represented the franchise as one of its best players, but as a fellow Puerto Rican, the honor hits close to home for Lindor.
"It's very inspiring. Someone that was close to me and to every Puerto Rican. Anybody that's Puerto Rican that makes it big, us Puerto Ricans feel like we made it as well," Lindor said in the clubhouse prior to Saturday's game. "To be on the biggest stages, playoffs, All-Star games and to see him come back to the island is very special. We always talk about guys like that, like the Beltráns, [Roberto] Alomar, [Carlos] Delgado, [Ivan]Rodriguez. Guys that set the path for a guy like me today."
Lindor looked up to Beltrán because he was also a switch-hitter from the island, who played hard and "had swag," but he wouldn't get a chance to build a relationship with one of his idols until 2016.
Lindor, playing with Cleveland at the time, just wrapped up a series with the Beltrán's Yankees right before the All-Star break. The young shortstop was heading to San Diego for his first All-Star Game and shared a plane with the outfielder and a few other Yankees who also made the Midsummer Classic. That's when he had an opportunity to speak with the future Hall of Famer.
"Anybody that's from Puerto Rico and makes it big, us Puerto Ricans feel like we made it, as well."
Francisco Lindor says it was "very inspiring" to see Carlos Beltrán's success in Major League Baseball: pic.twitter.com/5QX8pUuM4n
"He's a mentor. Someone you can have a conversation with him, tell him the stuff I'm going through because he probably already went through it. He's helped me for sure," Lindor said of Beltrán. "I look up to him growing up and to have an opportunity to share the field with him. To have moments to talk to him. It's something I don't take for granted."
That relationship came in handy when Lindor was traded to the Mets in 2021. It was an adjustment period for Lindor, who struggled on and off the field. Going from a small market to New York City was tough for Lindor, but he had Beltrán to help him.
Beltran got Lindor in touch with a realtor and helped him with the off-the-field transition, but also offered a shoulder when the on-the-field production wasn't there.
"When I first got traded here, I called him and I talked to him," Lindor said. "I didn't play well. I sucked in the beginning and having him there to comfort me and say, 'Hey, this stuff is going to happen. It's ok. You're going to go through stuff like this, but you're going to come out on the other side. Stay true to yourself and play the game the right way.'
"Stuff like that early on was huge for me today."
Five years later, and Lindor has become an important part of the team on the field and as a locker room leader.
"I love Francisco. I admire him. I love the way he plays. I always watch the switch-hitters in the game," Beltrán said prior to his number retirement ceremony. "He will be in this position at some point in life. I'm grateful for the friendship that we have...We have a good relationship. We talk about baseball, we talk about hitting, life, family, we talk about kids, we talk about everything.
"The relationship I was able to build with him is a friendship more than anything else."
Could that relationship-building help Beltrán get a managerial job with the Mets or elsewhere? Lindor was asked and the shortstop is convinced the Hall of Famer will succeed in that realm if that's his desire.
"If he wants it. I believe he'll succeed whenever he becomes a manager," Lindor said. "If the organization feels that's the right fit for us…. If he decides to pursue, and if they feel he's the best fit, he'll succeed at it.
"To be a manager is not about respect, it's about knowing the game, making the right moves at the right time and connecting with players. And I think he can do all those."
"I love Francisco. I admire him. I love the way he plays. Being a switch-hitter, I'm always watching the switch-hitters in the game. He will be in this position at some point in life."
- Carlos Beltrán on Francisco Lindor pic.twitter.com/gwQGCW2KP5

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Juan Soto hit a three-run homer and the New York Mets kept the Philadelphia Phillies from gaining ground in the National League wild-card race with a 6-3 victory Friday night.
Edmundo Sosa went 3 for 3 with a home run and a double for the Phillies (85-69), who remained tied with the Cubs for the top two wild-card spots after Chicago lost 6-4 to Cincinnati. Both teams began the day one game ahead of the San Diego Padres, who were scheduled to host Miami later Friday.
Derek Hill also went deep and Bryson Stott had an RBI double for Philadelphia.
Soto also doubled and finished with three hits. A.J. Ewing’s two-run single capped a three-run first inning for the last-place Mets, who ended a five-game losing streak — their longest under interim manager Andy Green. Carson Benge had an RBI single in the first and reached base three times.
Francisco Lindor remained at 299 career homers after going 2 for 5 with a double.
Rookie left-hander Zac Thornton (5-5) allowed two runs and five hits in six innings. He struck out four and walked one. Thornton has permitted two runs or fewer eight times in 14 big league starts.
Dedniel Núñez got four outs for his second career save and first since July 13, 2024.
José Urquidy tossed 4 2/3 innings of scoreless bulk relief in his Phillies debut. Urquidy, designated for assignment by the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday, was claimed off waivers Thursday.
Phillies opener Tim Mayza (3-4) was charged with three runs. He threw 33 pitches but recorded just one out — the shortest outing by a Philadelphia starter since Cristopher Sánchez got only one out against the Washington Nationals on July 29, 2021.
Up next
The Mets will retire the No. 15 jersey worn by Hall of Fame center fielder Carlos Beltrán on Saturday before RHP Christian Scott (4-5, 3.76 ERA) opposes Phillies RHP Andrew Painter (3-9, 5.54).

item.content:encoded:
The Mets (70-84) defeated the Philadelphia Phillies (85-69) by a score of 6-3.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Mets left-handed starter Zac Thornton plunked leadoff batter Kyle Schwarber on a 3-2 count to get the game started. The rookie battled back, striking out Trea Turner and Bryce Harper before Mets first baseman Brett Baty made a diving stop on a Luis Arraez grounder down the line to put away the third out.
-- Southpaw Tim Mayza served as the bullpen opener for Philadelphia, and Francisco Lindor jumped all over him with a leadoff double. With one out, Bo Bichette worked a 10-pitch at-bat, culminating in a single to center field which moved Lindor up to third base. Carson Benge kept the line moving and drove in Lindor with an opposite-field single. Mark Vientos was walked to load the bases, and Phillies manager Don Mattingly pulled Mayza for right-handed reliever Jose Urquidy. A.J. Ewing roped an Urquidy fastball for a double, which scored two runs. Urquidy retired the next two Mets batters to limit the damage to three runs.
-- In the second inning, Ewing got turned around on a deep line drive to center, failing to haul in the RBI double for Bryson Stott, which cut the Mets' lead to 3-1. In the bottom half of the inning, Juan Soto doubled into the left-center field gap with two outs, but Urquidy struck out Bichette to end the threat.
-- With two outs away in the top of the sixth, Phillies left fielder Edmundo Sosa blasted a solo shot to left field, his third hit of the night. Excluding Sosa, Thornton allowed just two hits. He struck out four and walked one, allowing two earned runs across 87 pitches.
-- Soto took a hanging breaking ball thrown by Phillies right-hander Orion Kerkering 428 feet for a two-out three-run homer in the bottom of the sixth. Soto's 26th tater of 2026 put the Mets up 6-2.
-- Philadelphia center fielder Derek Hill responded with a solo home run off of Mets left-handed reliever Nate Lavender in the top of the seventh. Lavender persevered, retiring each of the next four batters he faced, before handing the ball to Dedniel Núñez to record the third out of the eighth. In the bottom half of the frame, Bichette grounded into a double play with the bases loaded. Núñez handled the ninth inning and retired the side to earn the first save of his season - and second save of his career - to seal the 6-3 win for the Mets.
Game MVP: Juan Soto
Soto notched his third game with multiple extra-base hits in September, going 3-for-5 with a double and a three-run homer. It was also Soto's third game of the season with at least three hits.
Highlights
What's next
The Mets play the Phillies in the third game of the four-game home series on Saturday at 4:10 p.m. on SNY. They will honor 2026 Baseball Hall of Fame inductee Carlos Beltrán.
New York will send out Christian Scott (3.76 ERA, 1.26 WHIP in 105.1 IP).
Philadelphia is set to start fellow right-hander Andrew Painter (5.54 ERA, 1.44 WHIP in 115.1 IP).
